lesson.title: Trust, But Verify: Sanity Checks with assert
lesson.summary: The assert statement checks a boolean condition the programmer believes must always be true and raises AssertionError immediately if it isn't, but it's a debugging aid, not a substitute for validating real input.
lesson.body:
raise and custom exceptions are for conditions a program needs to handle gracefully, like a user typing a negative age. assert exists for a different purpose: catching the programmer's own mistakes. When you write a function and you are confident a certain condition must hold at a certain point, if it does not, you have made a logic error somewhere, assert is the tool for saying so directly in the code, in a way that stops execution immediately and points right at the assumption that broke.

```python
def average(numbers):
    assert len(numbers) > 0, "numbers must not be empty"
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)

print(average([10, 20, 30]))
average([])
```

assert evaluates the boolean expression len(numbers) > 0. For average([10, 20, 30]), len(numbers) is 3, so 3 > 0 is True, the assertion passes silently, and the function continues on to sum(numbers) / len(numbers), which is 60 / 3, giving 20.0, printed by the outer print(). For average([]), len(numbers) is 0, so 0 > 0 is False, and the assertion fails, immediately raising AssertionError with the text after the comma as its message:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
AssertionError: numbers must not be empty
```

The syntax is assert, followed by a boolean expression, the same kind already used in if statements and while loops, and optionally a comma and a message. If the expression is truthy, nothing visible happens at all and execution simply continues past it. If it is falsy, Python raises AssertionError with the optional message attached, and like any other exception it can technically be caught with a try-except block, though assertions are usually left uncaught on purpose, since the whole point is to stop and expose the bug rather than quietly paper over it.

Here is the real caveat worth remembering. Python can be run in an optimized mode, using the -O flag, and in that mode every assert statement in the entire program is stripped out and never runs at all, as if it had never been written. That is a deliberate design choice: assertions are meant to be a free safety net during development that can be switched off in production, not a guaranteed check. Because of that, assert should never be used to validate real, untrusted input, like data typed by a user or received over a network. Checking a user's age for validity belongs in an if statement that raises a real exception, as covered a couple of lessons back, since that check always runs no matter how the program is started. assert belongs to sanity checks on your own internal assumptions, conditions that, if false, mean there is a bug in your code, not a bad user.
